explanation: The prefrontal cortex controls personality, social behavior, and executive functions. A lawyer losing interest in work and not caring about family indicates damage to the prefrontal area, consistent with frontal lobe trauma.
keyConcept: Prefrontal lesion causes personality/behavior changes

explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum. It originates from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus) and enters through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries upper limb proprioception

explanation: The anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle. It decussates twice (once at the level of entry and once before entering the cerebellum).
keyConcept: Anterior spinocerebellar enters via superior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: The posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It does not decussate.
keyConcept: Posterior spinocerebellar tract via inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract which carries proprioceptive feedback from the lower limbs to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains ventral spinocerebellar

explanation: The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral cerebellar nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellar cortex (particularly the lateral parts) and projects via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the thalamus and red nucleus.
keyConcept: Dentate nucleus is most lateral, projects via SCP

explanation: The dentate nucleus is the main output nucleus of the neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres). It projects inhibitory fibers via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral thalamus (VPL/VPM) and red nucleus.
keyConcept: Dentate nucleus projects neocerebellar efferent

explanation: The neocerebellum (lateral parts of posterior lobe) is anatomically located in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum. It is concerned with planning and executing voluntary movements, particularly those requiring skilled precision.
keyConcept: Neocerebellum in posterior lobe

explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes the medulla oblongata, pons, and cerebellum. The crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (not hindbrain), containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
keyConcept: Crus cerebri is midbrain, not hindbrain

explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is attached to the lower border of the pons, in the groove between the pons and pyramid of the medulla. It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at the pontomedullary junction.
keyConcept: Abducent nerve at lower pons above pyramid

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to attach to the posterior (dorsal) surface of the brain stem. It emerges from the posterior aspect of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus.
keyConcept: Trochlear nerve is only CN from posterior brainstem

explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a space between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents include the oculomotor nerve, mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, posterior perforated substance, and cerebral peduncles. The anterior perforated substance is lateral to the optic tract, not in the interpeduncular fossa.
keyConcept: Anterior perforated substance not in interpeduncular fossa

explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is attached at the cerebellopontine angle, along with the facial nerve. This is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and olive where these nerves emerge.
keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle

explanation: The lateral recess is the only true recess of the fourth ventricle. It extends laterally beneath the superior cerebellar peduncle and opens at the foramen of Luschka into the subarachnoid space.
keyConcept: Lateral recess is a recess of fourth ventricle

explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The facial colliculus (a elevation) is formed by the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers looping around it.
keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus

explanation: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle is continuous with the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
keyConcept: Superior 4th ventricle angle leads to cerebral aqueduct

explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is attached to the lateral surface of the pons, at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle. The abducent nerve attaches at the lower border, and facial/vestibulocochlear at the cerebellopontine angle.
keyConcept: Trigeminal attaches at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

explanation: The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies posterior to the brain stem and is not considered part of it, though it is connected by three peduncles.
keyConcept: Cerebellum not part of brain stem

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve rootlets emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the pyramid and olive. This is the anterior surface of the medulla.
keyConcept: CN XII between pyramid and olive

explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: CN IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges at the pontomedullary junction, close to the median plane (between the pons and pyramid). It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at this junction.
keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial at pontomedullary junction

explanation: The facial colliculus is a bump in the floor of the fourth ventricle formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve wrapping around it. It lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea.
keyConcept: Facial colliculus between limbs of inferior fovea

explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers that loop around it (the facial nerve genu). This creates a prominence in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
keyConcept: Facial colliculus overlies abducent nucleus

explanation: The facial colliculus is formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve (motor root) that curve around it internally. These fibers form the facial nerve genu in the brainstem.
keyConcept: Facial colliculus formed by CN VI nucleus and CN VII fibers

explanation: The posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by the cerebral peduncles. These are two large bundles of descending fibers on either side of the midbrain.
keyConcept: Cerebral peduncles form posterolateral boundary
